rating_explained: The story asserts Tuberville told Raw Story's Matt Laslo he reads 'very little' to keep his own opinion, then asked 'Did they ban Politico, too?' when pressed about reporting that JD Vance was the source behind a story the White House cited to justify banning Politico, and said 'I didn't see that' about ProPublica's report that a Kremlin-linked oligarch financed Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding. A second outlet (All Chronology) corroborates the 'I read very little... I want my own opinion, not somebody else's' quote to Laslo, along with his 'no way Vance would do that' and 'I don't get into all that' responses. ProPublica's investigation confirms Umar Kremlev, an oligarch close to Vladimir Putin, footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of Trump Jr.'s wedding expenses, based on records reviewed and interviews with three people familiar with the event. The Crosscheck's fact-check confirms Trump banned Politico (alongside CNN and MS NOW) from the White House on September 18 and that a September 22 court letter cited six Politico stories; it rates the Vance-as-source identification as single-sourced from Status and unproven, though undenied. The ban itself was real, Tuberville's quoted answers match across independent accounts, and the ProPublica reporting is described faithfully, so the claim holds.

rating_explained: The story asserts a new campaign ad spotlights Sen. Roger Marshall's aggressive medical-debt collection record: 700+ patient lawsuits, 81 arrests after missed court dates, including a woman arrested in 2011 over a missed $50 payment while eight months pregnant. The ad's existence and content are confirmed by the Washington Examiner's reporting that Democratic Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton released a video ad featuring former patient 'Meischa' saying she was arrested because she 'didn't make a $50 payment to Roger Marshall' while eight months pregnant, and by a YouTube short describing the ad's content. Marshall's side is on record disputing the framing: his spokeswoman said the procedures matched standard Kansas practice and his lawyer said he was not involved in warrant or arrest decisions. The ad exists, its account matches the NYT findings, and Marshall's rebuttal is noted; the claim is accurate.
